language.script_notes: Spanish nationwide; over 20 Mayan languages are spoken locally (K'iche', Kaqchikel and others), rarely appearing on formal signage. City streets are gridded, with one-way streets marked 'Una Vía' and two-way streets marked 'Doble Vía'.

road_furniture.bollard_color: Yellow-and-black striped bollards where present, but bollards are extremely rare overall.
road_furniture.curb_style: Cobblestone streets in colonial towns such as Antigua; painted kerbs in cities.
road_furniture.km_marker_style: Utility poles are most often painted red at the bottom — a useful Guatemala tell. Texaco, Puma and Uno are common fuel-station brands.

architecture.roof_style: Red clay tile pitched roofs in colonial towns; flat concrete roofs on much modern construction; corrugated metal common in rural areas.
architecture.roof_material: Red clay tile in colonial areas, corrugated metal and flat concrete elsewhere.
architecture.wall_construction: Spanish colonial Baroque architecture with colourful facades and cobblestone streets in Antigua (UNESCO World Heritage site, set against three volcanoes); concrete-block construction in Guatemala City and most towns; traditional adobe and simple block houses in the highland Maya villages.
architecture.wall_color_palette: Vivid yellow, ochre, blue and terracotta colonial facades in Antigua; brightly painted concrete shopfronts; earthy tones in rural highland villages.
architecture.distinctive_building_types: Colonial churches and ruins (Antigua); ancient Maya temples and pyramids in the Petén rainforest (Tikal); brightly painted 'chicken buses' (converted US school buses) as an iconic moving landmark; dense concrete Guatemala City neighbourhoods.

nature.vegetation: Dense tropical rainforest in the northern Petén lowlands; cool pine and oak highland forest in the central mountains; tropical lowland farmland, banana and sugar cane on the Pacific plain.
nature.terrain: Mountainous and volcanic — the country has around 37 volcanoes, several of them active — with a fertile highland core, a hot Pacific coastal plain, and flat, jungle-covered lowlands in the north.
nature.climate_signature: Tropical but with a cooler 'eternal spring' feel at highland elevations; a wet, humid, dense-green look in the lowlands.

vehicles.plate_color: Small plates (roughly 15cm × 30cm) that don't fill the plate area on the car, in various colours by vehicle class.
vehicles.plate_format: Letter prefix indicating vehicle type followed by digits and letters (e.g. 'P 123ABC').
vehicles.distinctive_vehicles: Chicken buses — brightly painted, converted US school buses — are Guatemala's iconic vehicle; tuk-tuks in smaller towns; the Google Street View car carries a roof rack across the whole country, a very reliable Guatemala tell.

google_coverage.camera_generation: Mixed official Gen 3 coverage with the distinctive roof-rack car; the same car style (with a snorkel-like front fitting) is shared with a few other countries.
google_coverage.coverage_notes: Good coverage in the central highlands and main highways; sparser in the northern Petén and remote mountain areas.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Shared Maya highland culture and terrain, similar colonial architecture and colourful facades near the border
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Guatemala's roof-rack Google car appears across the entire country and is a very reliable tell; small Guatemalan plates and red-painted pole bases also help separate it from Mexico.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Shared Central American tropical vegetation, Spanish signage, similar concrete-block architecture and chicken-bus-style transport
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Guatemala's roof-rack Google car and its 'Una Vía'/'Doble Vía' street signage are strong tells; plate formats and road furniture also differ once compared directly.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Shared northern jungle border region and Maya heritage sites
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Belize is English-speaking and drives on the right with different plates and Caribbean-influenced architecture, whereas Guatemala's signage is in Spanish.
